These include behaviours such as compulsive checking reinforced by notifications, social expectations, and the possibility of new information and social feedback. Amirthalingam and Khera (2024) identify these as some of the many leading factors in social media’s setting for addiction.

These social media consumption statistics have since been updated. As of 2026, all of these statistics have increased by an estimated 10-20%. Additionally, there are now 5.16 billion active social media users worldwide, with 95% of children having a form of social media account, mainly TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, and Snapchat.

Digital natives describe the generation that grew up surrounded by digital technology. However, this does not lead to a greater implication of whether or not they have developed the appropriate skills to regulate the new set of habits formed within this environment. Most individuals under this term are still in adolescence, in which cognitive development is imperative in developing executive functions such as planning, impulse control, and decision-making.

The main takeaway from the casino analogy is the manner in which they reinforce learning and form an unpredictable reward system. Social media users receive this same kind of environment due to a lack of guarantee of reward (ie. a notification, an interesting post, a like, or a message). This is what leads to the behaviour of repeatedly checking one’s phone in the anticipation of a possible reward. De et al. (2025) expound on this further by their findings that internet addiction can cause a biological shift in the prefrontal cortex, leading to an increased sensitivity to stimuli whilst having reduced inhibitory control. This can lead to erratic decision-making and sudden emotional changes.

Reed Hastings, Netflix’ former CEO had stated that “Sleep is my greatest enemy” in reference to the growth of the company, not only focusing on his direct competitors but looking at what he can capitalise on a user’s day. This point introduces the commercial incentive behind the persuasion of digital technology. These platforms benefit from sustained user engagement and aim to maximise profit, which proves to cause significant ethical concerns when they are aimed towards adolescents. There is a conflict between the commercial engagement goals and the user’s wellbeing, wherein they benefit from an algorithm that does not keep individuals’ mental health at the forefront of importance.

This anecdote illustrates how problematic use can develop gradually, becoming notable only after it begins to interfere with daily routines and relationships if suddenly stopped. This is then connected to the concept of “fear of missing out” (FOMO), the anxiety that other people are having rewarding experiences without you. This desire may be disconnected from a person's individual feelings of whether or not they actually want to be there, and is then overcome by the fear of what would happen if they were not. Studies conducted by De et al. found that adolescents who experienced this were more prone to social media addiction (while in addition negatively affecting their quality of sleep).

This section can be connected to the relationship between digital behaviour, social connection, and psychological wellbeing. The problematic use of social media may then start to interfere with the user’s offline relationships when it displaces meaningful interaction, especially when social comparison and feedback-seeking may contribute to further distress. However, online communication can also strengthen friendships and provide support, particularly for people who feel isolated offline. The impact therefore depends on the quality and context of the interaction, not simply the amount of time spent on a screen. The creation of an online space means complexities and nuances for different types of dynamics, and it is now a matter of identifying them to better understand their effects on people.
